newsitem.title: UK: IRA chiefs may be planning ceasefire, say UK papers.
newsitem.headline: IRA chiefs may be planning ceasefire, say UK papers.

text.p: The IRA's top leaders plan to meet for the first time in 10 years in a move that could herald an end to the guerrilla group's violent 27-year campaign to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, according to newspaper reports.
Several Sunday newspapers said the IRA's shadowy General Army Convention (GAC) would meet as early as next month -- 10 years after its last gathering -- to decide policy for the years ahead.
"If the Army Convention were to meet now, it would almost certainly be to seek endorsement of a formal announcement that the IRA campaign is over," the Observer said.

The Sunday Express said the Irish Republican Army, which broke an 18-month truce in February with a series of bomb attacks in Britain, could even be ready to give up some of its weapons as a gesture to gain entry for its political wing, Sinn Fein, to talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
"The IRA is on the brink of another ceasefire -- and this time it could be permanent," the paper said.

The GAC is made up of delegates from all the IRA's units, commands, brigades and battalions as well as figures from the organisation's executive committee and general headquarters, according to the Sunday Times.
"It is the IRA's supreme authority and the only body with the power to declare permanent peace," the paper said.

It said senior Irish police, aware of a proliferation of local IRA meetings to select delegates, believed the GAC was likely to produce either a ceasefire or the offer of one under certain conditions.
The reports help explain the upbeat assessment that Irish Prime Minister John Bruton gave last week of the prospects for the peace process in Northern Ireland.

Bruton, on a visit to Washington, said he had reason to hope conditions might exist in which the IRA could call a new ceasefire. "I receive information that gives me grounds to be optimistic," he said.
The Sunday Express quoted a British government official as sharing optimism for a fresh breakthrough.

But the paper also cautioned that, in the eyes of some Irish Republican insiders, the rosy reports were being spread by Bruton and British Prime Minister John Major to put pressure on the IRA to announce a ceasefire.
The Sunday Times added that British authorities feared that any GAC meeting would be preceded by IRA attacks on targets in England.
